current_text: [Appraise Goods] — Four cycles of manifests list the tin and the salt packed with it on one line, and the salt is perishable household stock where the tin is not. Under form nine, clause four, that stock carries an exemption from queue hold — and one manifest line puts the crate inside it.
The forms are stacked in filing order, oldest at the bottom — appraise the stack and the clause comes out of it.
Tier stamps on the jar shoulders. Half of them are numbers your permit does not reach. The keeper watches you read them and goes back to her tally.
Bar stock in strapped bundles, sorted by gauge. Wrist-thick at the bottom of the rack, pencil-thin at the top. The paper tag on each bundle gives a tier number and a bench number.
Cooled slag and cracked crucible shards, heaped to just under a line painted on the flagstones around the pile. Fresh paint on the line, the brush marks still crisp at the edges.
You lean on the bronze rail. Warm brass under your palm; from the shaft, cold air and the clank of the cage somewhere below.
The rack by the second bench is hung with numbered slips. Below the number, three lines to a slip: stock number, bench number, hour. Not one carries a name.
A wide iron-strapped door wedged open on the sill, and past it the hall runs hotter and louder than the tier does.
You walk the pallet the last hand's width onto the loading square and square the strapping after it. The attendant looks at the load, then writes an hour beside it on the cage slate.
The bench ticks twice under your hand as it cools, and the racks above it are empty down to the pegs.
A bronze floor grate breathing white steam in slow pushes. The flags around it carry a beat you can feel through your boots.

A Drake in a leather apron scarred through in three places, both forearms banded with old burn-marks. Her eyes stay on the colour of the billet; her free hand finds the tongs without going to look for them.

The lift coat is brass-buttoned to the throat, and the Drake wearing it keeps one hand along the gate lever without closing on it. He calls the quarter bell a beat before the cage comes up into the frame.
The gauge on the bench is reading in marks you do not know. Setting the count by guess would spoil the billet and the week of work in it.
Colour and quench you can read off the billet yourself. The count between them takes a trained eye — appraise it and the numbers come clear.
Two thumbprints gone grey in the margin of the examination standard. The examiner's seal is down in the corner, the sheet pinned at eye height.
A scum ring goes right around the inside of the tub three fingers above the water, and the water below it is grey with scale under an unbroken skin of oil.
A grid of finished pieces the width of the wall, one to a slot. Each has a wired civic tag on it, giving a smith's mark and a measure but no price.
The rig overshoots its marks and settles wrong, then does it again while you watch. The smith has not asked you to put a hand on it.
[Eagle Eyes] — The haze thins: nine tiers of stall rows and patrol routes below the rail. Two floors down, a dropped coin purse sits on a ledge with its drawstring still knotted.
The haze has closed back over the tiers below; come back to the rail after a night's sleep.
[Low-Grade Synthesis] — You hold it over a low flame until the colour settles, then cork it cloudy and most of the way to a proper draught.
A grey wash sits half-way up the dark glass, the coals beneath it cold. Reducing it to salts is a distiller's job, not yours.
Xif's own bench, the burner under it already lit. You have no true synthesis to put over that flame.
The bench Xif keeps for himself. Clean glass in a rack, two empty measures set side by side at the front edge. The blue flame under it burns without a flicker.
Low carts for hire in a rank, shafts down on the stone. A tier number and a rate are chalked on every tailboard. The queue board at the head of the rank stands with no one at it.
First of three stalls in a row, and the counter comes to the same height as the next two. A civic inspector's initials are burned into the corner post.
You put your weight on the ledge, and on the far side of the glass a clerk stamps a form, drops it beside her inkwell and rings the bell.
